questions.stem: A Python Lambda function depends on a library with compiled native code. The developer packaged the dependencies on a macOS laptop, and the function fails to import the library in Lambda. What should the developer do?

options.text: Increase the function's memory
options.rationale: Memory does not fix a binary built for the wrong platform.

options.text: Move the macOS-built dependencies into a Lambda layer and attach it to the function
options.rationale: A layer built the same way has the same incompatible binaries.

options.text: Add the library's name to an environment variable
options.rationale: Environment variables do not install or load libraries.

options.text: Build the package in a Lambda-compatible container with sam build --use-container
options.rationale: Native code must be compiled for the Lambda execution environment's operating system and architecture.

questions.explanation: Dependencies with native code must match Lambda's Linux runtime; building in a container is the simplest way.

questions.stem: An Amazon ECR repository fills up with old, untagged images left over from builds. The team wants them removed automatically. What should the developer configure?

options.text: An ECR lifecycle policy that expires untagged images
options.rationale: Lifecycle policies clean up images by age, count or tag status.

options.text: An S3 Lifecycle rule on the bucket that stores the repository's images
options.rationale: ECR manages image storage itself; S3 Lifecycle rules do not apply to repositories.

options.text: Tag immutability on the repository
options.rationale: Immutability stops tags being overwritten; it does not delete images.

options.text: Image scanning on push
options.rationale: Scanning finds vulnerabilities; it does not remove images.

questions.explanation: Use ECR lifecycle policies to keep repositories tidy and reduce storage costs.

questions.stem: Deployments must always run the exact container image that passed testing, and nobody should be able to replace an image under an existing tag. Which actions will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Turn on image scanning for the repository
options.rationale: Scanning finds vulnerabilities; it does not stop a tag from being overwritten.

options.text: Tag each image with a unique value, such as the Git commit ID
options.rationale: A unique tag points to one specific build.

options.text: Push every build to the same tag
options.rationale: Reusing one tag makes it impossible to tell which build is deployed.

options.text: Enable tag immutability on the ECR repository
options.rationale: Immutable tags cannot be overwritten by a later push.

options.text: Deploy the latest tag in every environment so they run the same build
options.rationale: latest moves with each push, so environments may run different, untested builds.

questions.explanation: Unique, immutable tags make deployments reproducible.

questions.stem: A container image for a compiled application includes the full build toolchain, which makes the image large. The toolchain is not needed at runtime. How should the developer change the Dockerfile?

options.text: Add a final RUN step that compresses the toolchain files inside the existing image layers
options.rationale: Image layers are immutable once created, so a later step cannot remove the toolchain from the earlier layers.

options.text: Use a multi-stage build that copies the compiled output into a slim final image
options.rationale: The build stage keeps the tools, and the final stage contains only what runs.

options.text: Push the image to two ECR repositories
options.rationale: Duplicating the image does not make it smaller.

options.text: Turn on tag immutability
options.rationale: Immutability affects tags, not image size.

questions.explanation: Multi-stage builds separate build-time dependencies from the runtime image.

questions.stem: A build server runs docker push to an Amazon ECR repository and gets an error that it has no basic auth credentials. What should the build run first?

options.text: aws ecr create-repository with the same name as the image
options.rationale: Creating a repository does not authenticate Docker.

options.text: docker build with the --no-cache option
options.rationale: Rebuilding the image does not supply credentials.

options.text: aws ecr get-login-password, piped to docker login for the registry
options.rationale: Docker needs an ECR authorization token before it can push.

options.text: aws configure set region to the repository's AWS Region before the push
options.rationale: A Region setting alone does not log Docker in to the registry.

questions.explanation: Docker clients authenticate to ECR with a temporary token from get-login-password.

questions.stem: Several teams publish internal npm packages and also use public packages from npmjs.com. The company wants one private place to fetch both. Which service should the developer use?

options.text: Amazon ECR
options.rationale: ECR stores container images, not npm packages.

options.text: An Amazon S3 bucket with a folder for each package and its published versions
options.rationale: S3 can hold files but does not work as an npm registry.

options.text: AWS CodeBuild
options.rationale: CodeBuild runs builds; it does not host packages.

options.text: AWS CodeArtifact, with an external connection to the public npm registry
options.rationale: CodeArtifact hosts private packages and can proxy and cache public ones.

questions.explanation: CodeArtifact is a managed package repository for npm, PyPI, Maven and more.

questions.stem: A team wants to turn a new feature on or off for users without redeploying the application, and to roll the change out gradually with automatic rollback if alarms go off. Which service fits?

options.text: AWS AppConfig
options.rationale: AppConfig deploys configuration and feature flags with deployment strategies and alarm-based rollback.

options.text: AWS CloudFormation
options.rationale: CloudFormation provisions infrastructure; changing a flag would mean a stack update.

options.text: Lambda environment variables
options.rationale: Changing an environment variable updates the function and is not gradual.

options.text: Amazon ECR
options.rationale: ECR stores container images, not runtime flags.

questions.explanation: The clues are no redeploy, a gradual rollout and alarm-based rollback, which AppConfig deployment strategies provide. Lambda environment variables are the nearest distractor, but changing one updates the function and is not gradual.

questions.stem: The same application code runs in dev, test and prod. Each environment has its own database URL and settings. How can the developer store these values so the code can load the right set?

options.text: Store all environments' values in one JSON parameter and parse the right section in code
options.rationale: This mixes environments and makes access control harder.

options.text: Store them in Parameter Store under a path per environment and read them by path
options.rationale: Parameter hierarchies group settings, and GetParametersByPath loads one environment's set.

options.text: Hardcode the values and pick them with a build flag
options.rationale: Hardcoded settings need a new build to change.

options.text: Store them as tags on the application's IAM role
options.rationale: Role tags are for access control, not application configuration.

questions.explanation: Parameter Store hierarchies are a simple way to keep environment-specific configuration.

questions.stem: A developer added a new resource to a REST API in the Amazon API Gateway console, but clients calling the prod stage URL get errors for the new path. What did the developer miss?

options.text: Enabling caching on the stage
options.rationale: Caching is optional and does not publish changes.

options.text: Creating a usage plan
options.rationale: Usage plans meter and throttle clients.

options.text: Deploying the API to the prod stage
options.rationale: Changes take effect for clients only after the API is deployed to a stage.

options.text: Adding a custom domain name for the stage
options.rationale: The stage URL already works without a custom domain.

questions.explanation: A deployment is a snapshot of the API; each stage serves one deployment.

questions.stem: A REST API in Amazon API Gateway must be reachable only from inside the company's VPC. Which combination of steps will meet this requirement? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Make the API private, with a resource policy that allows the VPC endpoint
options.rationale: A private API is inaccessible until its resource policy grants access to specific VPCs or VPC endpoints.

options.text: Create the API as an edge-optimized API served through CloudFront
options.rationale: Edge-optimized APIs are public and served through CloudFront locations.

options.text: Create a gateway VPC endpoint for API Gateway and add it to the route tables
options.rationale: Gateway endpoints exist only for Amazon S3 and DynamoDB; API Gateway uses interface endpoints.

options.text: Use a Regional API with a custom domain name
options.rationale: A custom domain does not make a public API private.

options.text: Create an interface VPC endpoint for API Gateway (execute-api) in the VPC
options.rationale: The endpoint gives the VPC a private path to API Gateway through AWS PrivateLink.

questions.explanation: A private API is reached through an interface VPC endpoint for execute-api, and its resource policy must allow that endpoint or VPC. A gateway endpoint is the nearest distractor, but gateway endpoints exist only for Amazon S3 and DynamoDB.

questions.stem: A developer zips a Node.js Lambda function's index.js file and deploys it. Every invocation fails with "Cannot find module 'uuid'". The function works on the developer's laptop. What should the developer do?

options.text: Add uuid to the function's environment variables in the console
options.rationale: Environment variables hold settings, not code modules.

options.text: Increase the function's memory so that npm can install the module at startup
options.rationale: Lambda does not run npm install; memory is not the issue.

options.text: Change the function's runtime to the latest Node.js version
options.rationale: Changing the runtime version does not add the function's third-party dependencies; they must be in the deployment package or a layer.

options.text: Include the node_modules folder with the uuid package in the .zip file
options.rationale: Lambda runs only what is in the deployment package (and its layers), so dependencies must be packaged.

questions.explanation: A Lambda .zip package must contain the function's dependencies, or get them from a layer.

questions.stem: Builds of the same commit sometimes produce different dependency versions, because the build installs whatever versions are newest that day. The team wants every build of a commit to use the same dependency versions. What should the developer do?

options.text: Commit the lock file, and install with npm ci in the build
options.rationale: npm ci installs exactly the versions recorded in the lock file and fails if they do not match package.json.

options.text: Run npm update on every build so that dependencies move to the newest allowed versions
options.rationale: Moving to the newest versions on each build is the cause of the drift.

options.text: Delete the lock file so that it does not conflict with package.json
options.rationale: Without the lock file, each build resolves versions again.

options.text: Build the dependencies once a week on a schedule and reuse them
options.rationale: This hides the drift for a week but still lets versions change between rebuilds.

questions.explanation: Reproducible builds pin dependency versions with a committed lock file.

questions.stem: A REST API in Amazon API Gateway has dev and prod stages. Each stage must call a different alias (dev or prod) of the same Lambda function, without separate API definitions. Which combination of steps will meet this requirement? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Point the integration at $LATEST and branch on the stage in the code
options.rationale: This loses the separation that aliases give between dev and prod versions.

options.text: Grant API Gateway permission to invoke each alias in the function's resource policy
options.rationale: Each alias is a separate resource, so each needs its own invoke permission.

options.text: Set an environment variable on the function that names the stage
options.rationale: The function cannot change which alias API Gateway calls.

options.text: Use a stage variable for the alias name in the Lambda integration's function ARN
options.rationale: Each stage sets the variable, so one integration calls a different alias per stage.

options.text: Create a separate copy of the API definition for each stage
options.rationale: This is what the requirement wants to avoid.

questions.explanation: Stage variables let one API definition call stage-specific backends such as Lambda aliases.

questions.stem: A team stores feature settings in AWS AppConfig. Last week a teammate deployed a configuration with a typo in a JSON field name, which broke the application. How can the team catch this before a configuration is deployed?

options.text: Turn on versioning in the hosted configuration store
options.rationale: Versions help roll back but do not check a configuration before it is deployed.

options.text: Add a JSON Schema validator to the configuration profile
options.rationale: AppConfig runs validators before a deployment starts and stops it if the configuration fails validation.

options.text: Use the AllAtOnce deployment strategy for every configuration change
options.rationale: Deploying everywhere at once spreads a bad configuration faster.

options.text: Store the configuration in Amazon S3 instead of the AppConfig store
options.rationale: Moving the source does not add validation.

questions.explanation: AppConfig validators (JSON Schema or a Lambda function) check configurations before deployment.

questions.stem: A Dockerfile copies the whole project and then runs npm install. Every small source change reinstalls all dependencies, so image builds are slow. How should the developer reorder the Dockerfile?

options.text: Run npm install after the CMD instruction at the end of the file
options.rationale: Instructions after CMD still run at build time; this does not use the cache better.

options.text: Combine every instruction into a single RUN command
options.rationale: One large layer is rebuilt in full whenever anything changes.

options.text: Copy package.json and the lock file, run npm install, and then copy the source code
options.rationale: The dependency layer stays cached until package files change, so source edits rebuild only the later layers.

options.text: Use a larger base image that includes more system packages
options.rationale: A bigger base image does not help the dependency layer stay cached.

questions.explanation: Order Dockerfile steps from least to most frequently changed, to make the most of layer caching.

questions.stem: A team wants each container image to be checked for known software vulnerabilities as soon as it is pushed to an Amazon ECR repository. What should the developer turn on?

options.text: Tag immutability on the repository
options.rationale: Immutability stops tags from being overwritten; it does not scan images.

options.text: A lifecycle policy that expires untagged images
options.rationale: Lifecycle policies clean up images; they do not check them for vulnerabilities.

options.text: Cross-Region replication for the repository
options.rationale: Replication copies images to other Regions without scanning them.

options.text: Image scanning on push for the repository
options.rationale: ECR scans each image as it is pushed and reports findings on known vulnerabilities.

questions.explanation: ECR image scanning finds known vulnerabilities in container images.

questions.stem: Clients call a REST API in Amazon API Gateway through URLs such as https://abc123.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/prod. The company wants clients to use https://api.example.com/v1 instead, mapped to the prod stage. What should the developer set up?

options.text: A custom domain name with an API mapping from the v1 path to the prod stage
options.rationale: Custom domains give the API a friendly URL, and API mappings send a base path to a stage.

options.text: A Route 53 alias record that points directly at the execute-api URL
options.rationale: DNS alone does not make API Gateway accept requests for the custom host name.

options.text: A stage named v1 that is a copy of the prod stage
options.rationale: This changes the path on the default URL, not the host name.

options.text: A stage variable named domain set to api.example.com
options.rationale: Stage variables configure the stage's backends, not its public URL.

questions.explanation: Custom domain names and API mappings give APIs stable, friendly URLs.

questions.stem: An AWS CodeBuild project runs npm install against a private AWS CodeArtifact repository and fails with a 401 Unauthorized error. The build role has permission to use CodeArtifact. What should the build run before npm install?

options.text: npm login with an IAM user name and password for the account
options.rationale: CodeArtifact uses temporary tokens from AWS credentials, not IAM user names and passwords.

options.text: aws codeartifact login --tool npm
options.rationale: The login command gets a temporary token and configures npm to use the repository.

options.text: aws ecr get-login-password, piped to npm login
options.rationale: That command is for Amazon ECR registries.

options.text: npm cache clean, so that npm can try the request again
options.rationale: Clearing the cache does not add the missing authorization token.

questions.explanation: Package managers authenticate to CodeArtifact with a temporary token from aws codeartifact login or get-authorization-token.

questions.stem: A CloudFormation template creates an Amazon RDS database for several environments. The master password is currently a template parameter with a default value. The password must not appear in the template, and each environment has its own secret in AWS Secrets Manager. What should the developer do?

options.text: Keep the password parameter and set NoEcho to false on it
options.rationale: NoEcho false shows the value; the password would still be stored as a default.

options.text: Put the password in the template's Outputs section for each environment
options.rationale: Outputs are visible to anyone who can describe the stack.

options.text: Use a dynamic reference to the environment's Secrets Manager secret
options.rationale: A {{resolve:secretsmanager:...}} reference fetches the value at deploy time without putting it in the template.

options.text: Hardcode a different password in each environment's copy of the template
options.rationale: This puts the passwords in the templates.

questions.explanation: CloudFormation dynamic references pull secrets and parameters from Secrets Manager and Parameter Store at deploy time.
